description: We are a team of three enthusiastic students passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation. We are interested in planets, moons, Earth science, and space missions. Our team focuses on developing creative solutions using AI, web development, and digital tools. We welcome collaborative team members with skills in coding, hardware, web development, graphic design, photography, and space science who are eager to learn, share ideas, and build something innovative.
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based game that teaches students how real space missions are planned. Players take command of Lunar Outpost Alpha, a small moon base with four astronauts, and must keep them safe for seven mission days on a fixed budget. They balance three things: life support, electrical power and radiation protection. Nothing can be maxed out, because extra shielding costs budget and mass, and saving power can put the crew at risk. When a solar storm alert appears, the player decides whether to move the crew to a shelter, and the game explains why the choice helped or hurt.
The alerts are inspired by NASA's DONKI space-weather records, and the radiation lessons draw on LRO CRaTER research. This matters because students learn engineering trade-offs by deciding, failing and replaying, not by memorizing facts.
details:
What it does and how it works. The player picks solar panels, batteries and a shielding level within budget. Each mission day, the game updates life support and power. Random events, like a panel fault or a battery problem, test the player's backup plans. A solar particle alert forces a fast decision. A final report shows what worked, what failed and why.

Benefits. It's free, runs in any browser on a phone or computer, and needs no installation. Teachers can use it in class. Failure is treated as part of learning, and every ending comes with a short explanation.

Intended impact. We want students aged 10 to 16 to see that space missions are about balancing limited resources. Along the way they practise percentages, energy use, risk and critical thinking.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the game. CSS indicators or Chart.js for the dashboard. The NASA DONKI API for space-weather data. Local storage for saving mission records. GitHub Pages for hosting.

Creativity. Most space games focus on action. Ours focuses on engineering decisions and explains the reasons behind outcomes. It also separates NASA's real data from our own simplified game rules.

Factors we considered. We kept it simple for young players with only three core resources. The radiation model is clearly labelled as a simplified teaching model, not a real dose calculation, and all game numbers are documented as assumptions. We built the working core first and left extras for later.
